strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: whether manipulation policies can generalize from simple, randomly composed primitive objects ('Cézanne toys') to real-world objects, with a nice connection to cognitive science literature on infant development.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: zero-shot transfer evaluated in simulation (ManiSkill), on a real Franka arm with YCB objects, and on a Unitree H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands, providing evidence across multiple embodiments.

Strong empirical results: the 86M-parameter LEGO policy outperforms much larger VLA baselines (π0-FAST, OpenVA-OFT, 3B-7B parameters) in zero-shot settings despite being trained on only 1,500 demonstrations, and performs competitively with in-domain fine-tuned π0-FAST.

Thorough ablation studies: pooling mechanisms (DetPool vs. attention/CLS/mean pooling), scaling with number of toys and demos, model size, primitive types, toy complexity, and color diversity — the scaling analysis (demos matter more than toy diversity) is an interesting finding.

Excellent reproducibility and resources: code, checkpoints, dataset, detailed 3D printing settings, teleoperation setups, and evaluation protocols are documented in extensive appendices and released on the project page.
Honest limitations section and transparent reporting, including cases where a fine-tuned baseline outperforms their method.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of the core contribution: DetPool is essentially attention masking with mean pooling over object patch tokens, a straightforward and well-explored idea in object-centric vision; the main novelty is the training data recipe rather than the method.

Potential leakage undermining the 'trained only on random toys' claim: DetPool depends on SAM 2 and a Faster R-CNN detector trained on 200 manually annotated real toy images for deployment, so a component of the pipeline has seen real-object-like segmentation supervision; the paper does not ablate the sensitivity of results to mask quality or detector performance on unseen objects.

Baseline fairness concerns: VLA baselines are fine-tuned on very small toy datasets where they are known to overfit, and π0-FAST fine-tuned on their data actually outperforms LEGO on the real Franka benchmark (76.56% vs. 66.67%), which partially weakens the headline claim of outperforming state-of-the-art approaches.

Evaluation is limited to single-object, single-step grasping in a predefined grid; robustness to clutter, varied lighting, and harder object categories is not tested, and statistical significance/variance across trials is not reported (e.g., H1-2 results use only 5 trials per object, making 60% vs. 20% differences noisy).

Minor inconsistencies and presentation issues: abstract claims 67% success while Table 2 reports 66.67%; the text states the transformer is ViT-B sized while the appendix mentions ViT-L MVP; some claims about 'orders of magnitude' efficiency are somewhat exaggerated given the pretrained MVP encoder and SAM 2 dependency.

Scope of generalization claim is narrow: generalizing grasping across objects with a parallel gripper is a comparatively easy task relative to the paper's framing ('grasp anything'), and it remains unclear whether the findings extend to more complex manipulation skills.

strengths: The core idea is appealing and well-motivated: training exclusively on randomly assembled primitive 'toys' that are deliberately out-of-distribution, and testing zero-shot transfer to real YCB objects, is a clean and principled testbed for generalization in manipulation.

The evaluation spans simulation (ManiSkill), a real Franka arm (DROID setup), and a Unitree H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands, which is an unusually broad set of embodiments for a data-driven grasping paper.
Baselines include strong, recent VLA models (π₀-FAST, OpenVLA-OFT) and a training-free LLM approach (ShapeGrasp), with implementation details provided in the appendix.

The paper includes a reasonable set of ablations: pooling alternatives (attention/CLS/mean), number and diversity of toys, model size, primitive types, toy complexity, and color diversity, plus extensive reproducibility details (printing settings, hardware, teleoperation setups, code and data promised on the project page).
The method is lightweight (86M parameters) compared to 3B-7B VLA baselines, making the data-efficiency claim practically relevant.
weaknesses: The central attribution claim — that DetPool is 'the key' to generalization — is not fully supported. DetPool depends on SAM 2 (a powerful foundation segmentation model) at inference time, so a large share of the object-centric generalization may come from SAM rather than from the proposed mechanism or from the toy training data. There is no ablation isolating SAM's contribution (e.g., SAM-mask-based cropping without attention masking, or a no-mask baseline), making the headline 'crucial mechanism' claim potentially confounded.

The headline results are overstated relative to the actual numbers: on the real Franka benchmark, fine-tuned π₀-FAST achieves the best result (76.56% vs. LEGO's 66.67%), yet the abstract and introduction frame the contribution as outperforming state-of-the-art approaches. The strongest claim survives only against zero-shot baselines.

The task scope is narrow: single-object, single-step grasping of rigid objects on a predefined grid. Grasping is a relatively easy, well-studied task, and it is unclear whether the conclusions extend to articulated, deformable, or long-horizon manipulation; the limitations section acknowledges this but it substantially limits the significance of 'generalizable manipulation' claims.

Evaluation rigor is limited: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple training seeds are reported; the H1-2 evaluation uses only 13 objects with 5 trials each (65 trials), and the Franka evaluation restricts to a 'feasibly graspable' subset of YCB, which weakens statistical support for the reported gaps.

Evaluation consistency issues: the success-height threshold was lowered from 0.3 m to 0.15 m specifically for OpenVLA-OFT, an inconsistent protocol that could bias cross-method comparisons; the paper also claims π₀-FAST is 'too data hungry' for the small dataset without direct evidence.

Technical novelty is modest: composing objects from geometric primitives is a long-standing idea (the paper itself cites Marr & Nishihara 1978, Tulsiani et al. 2016, etc.), and DetPool is essentially attention masking plus mean pooling — a straightforward engineering technique. The cognitive-science motivation is evocative but the connection to the actual method is loose.

There are internal inconsistencies: the main text states the vision encoder is a ViT-B MVP backbone while Appendix E describes using an off-the-shelf ViT-L MVP model; the abstract reports 67% while Table 2 reports 66.67%; the amount of real demonstration data (500 vs. 1,500) is described inconsistently across sections for the H1-2 setting.

The baselines' poor performance on small toy datasets (e.g., OpenVLA-OFT degrading with more data) suggests possible under-tuning or hyperparameter mismatch rather than fundamental limitations of VLA scaling, and the paper's narrative against large-scale pretraining may partly reflect the difficulty of fine-tuning these models out of their training distribution rather than a genuine advantage of the proposed data recipe.

strengths: Interesting and well-motivated core idea: training exclusively on randomly assembled 'Cézanne toys' composed of four shape primitives, providing a principled OOD training set that transfers zero-shot to real-world objects, supported by an appealing cognitive-science motivation

Comprehensive and unusually thorough experimental evaluation spanning simulation (ManiSkill), a real Franka arm on 64 YCB objects, and a Unitree H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands, with a standardized grid-based evaluation protocol described in detail

Strong ablation and scaling studies: effect of number/diversity of demonstrations and toys, model size, primitive types, toy complexity, and color diversity, which substantiate the paper's claims about data efficiency and the importance of demonstration count

The proposed DetPool mechanism (attention masking on object patches + mean pooling) is simple, lightweight, applicable to any pretrained ViT, and the ablations (vs. attention/CLS/mean pooling) show a clear and consistent performance gain (22-48%)

Strong data-efficiency story: an 86M-parameter model trained from scratch on 1,500 demonstrations is competitive with or beats 3B-7B pretrained VLAs in zero-shot settings; code, checkpoints, and dataset are promised for release
Excellent reproducibility detail in the appendix: toy design/manufacturing, teleoperation setups, baseline finetuning recipes, and evaluation protocols are all documented
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: DetPool is essentially attention masking plus mean pooling over segmented patches, closely related to existing object-centric approaches (OTTER, Devin et al., instance-centric grasping); the difference from OTTER (applicability beyond CLIP) is incremental, and the central finding is more empirical than methodological

The abstract/intro claim of 'outperforming state-of-the-art approaches' is overstated: Table 2 shows finetuned π₀-FAST (76.56%) clearly beats LEGO (66.67%), and the abstract's '67%' does not match the reported 66.67% exactly

Baseline fairness is debatable: π₀-FAST and OpenVLA-OFT are large pretrained VLA models finetuned in a deliberately small-data regime where they are known to overfit; a comparison against data-efficient baselines matched in parameter count or against non-VLA generalization methods would strengthen the claim that DetPool (rather than architecture/regime) drives the gains

Dependence on segmentation masks at inference (SAM 2 for real images, a Faster R-CNN detector trained on 200 annotated images) introduces an extra failure mode and additional machinery not ablated; no analysis of how mask errors affect policy success

Single task scope: only single-step tabletop grasping is evaluated; generalization claims are confined to this task, and no failure-mode analysis or variance/error bars over evaluation trials are provided

Minor inconsistencies: Section 4.2/5.1 state ViT-Base/MVP ViT-T while Appendix E mentions ViT-L; some ablation numbers (e.g., Table 1 baselines dropping with more data) are discussed anecdotally without statistical rigor; Figure 4 left panel is hard to read

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated research question: testing whether a small set of primitive-composed 'toy' objects can drive zero-shot generalization to real-world objects, with a nice cognitive-science framing (Cézanne-style primitives, infant learning literature).

Extensive empirical evaluation across simulation (ManiSkill/YCB), a real Franka with gripper, and a Unitree H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands — broad embodiment coverage that is rare in most policy papers.

Strong data/compute efficiency story: an 86M-parameter model trained on ~1,500 real demonstrations is competitive with 3B–7B VLA baselines (π0-FAST, OpenVLA-OFT, DexGraspVLA, ShapeGrasp), which is a meaningful and practically relevant result.

Thorough ablations: pooling alternatives (attn/CLS/mean vs. DetPool), scaling with toy count and demos, model size, primitive types, toy complexity, Chamfer-distance analysis, and robustness to lighting, clutter, distractors, and mask noise (appendix).
High reproducibility: code, checkpoints, dataset, full 3D-printing parameters, teleoperation setups, and detailed baseline fine-tuning protocols are provided.
The H1-2 experiment (Table 3, 50.77% vs. ~18–26% for VLAs) is a convincing demonstration in an out-of-pretraining-distribution embodiment.
weaknesses: Modest technical novelty: DetPool (segmentation mask → attention masking → mean pooling over object patches) is a simple, incremental mechanism; the closest related work (OTTER, and object-centric grasping lines like Devin et al.) is acknowledged but the conceptual delta over mask-conditioned pooling is thin. The paper's contribution is primarily empirical rather than methodological.

Claim accuracy issues: Section 4.3 states LEGO is 'trained from scratch on only 1,500 demonstrations,' but the vision encoder is the pretrained MVP ViT-L, which was itself trained on robot manipulation data. This materially weakens the 'from scratch' and 'no pretraining' narrative and should be corrected.

Zero-shot claim is qualified by an implicit detection/segmentation dependency: DetPool requires a target-object mask (ground-truth in sim; SAM 2 + a Faster R-CNN trained on 200 hand-annotated toy images in the real world). The generalization of this detector itself to YCB objects is under-analyzed, and the mechanism for selecting which object to grasp in multi-object scenes is unclear — this partially undercuts the 'object-agnostic, zero-shot' framing.

Headline framing is somewhat overstated: on the real Franka benchmark, finetuned π0-FAST (76.56%) outperforms LEGO (66.67%); the abstract's 'outperforming state-of-the-art approaches' holds only for the zero-shot/non-DROID comparisons.

Baseline fairness concerns: the success threshold was lowered for OpenVLA-OFT (0.15 m vs. 0.3 m), and the very poor π0-FAST simulation results (4–8%) are explained only post-hoc ('data-hungry,' 'domain gap'), raising questions about hyperparameter tuning effort for baselines versus the proposed method.

Evaluation protocol limits scope: single-object tabletop grasping on a predefined grid; the claim that DetPool 'still allows the vision encoder to understand where the object is' via positional embeddings is asserted but not directly analyzed (e.g., no probing or visualization of the pooled representation), despite this being the paper's central mechanistic claim.

Some inconsistencies need cleanup: e.g., toy counts (27+35+38+47 = 147 multi-primitive toys vs. '250 diverse toys' total including primitives), and citation details (Ravi et al. 2024a/b ambiguity; Black et al. 2023 vs. 2024 for π0-FAST).

strengths: Interesting and well-motivated research question: whether training exclusively on randomly assembled primitive 'toys' can yield zero-shot generalization to real-world objects, with a nice connection to cognitive science literature.

The toy generation pipeline and dataset (250 compositional toys, 3D-printed, with sim and real teleoperated demonstrations) is a tangible resource, and the paper promises code, checkpoints, and dataset release, aiding reproducibility.
Comprehensive experimental coverage: simulation on ManiSkill, real Franka on YCB (64 objects x 16 placements), and a second embodiment (Unitree H1-2 with dexterous hands) on 13 everyday objects.

Extensive ablations: pooling alternatives, model size, primitive types, toy complexity, geometric similarity (Chamfer distance), condition/prediction lengths, control modes, toy color, and robustness analyses (lighting, clutter, distractors, mask noise).
DetPool is lightweight and is shown to substantially outperform standard mean/CLS/attention pooling baselines in simulation, supporting the object-centric representation hypothesis.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of the core contribution: DetPool is essentially an attention mask from a segmentation model plus mean pooling over object patches. This is a straightforward engineering combination, closely related to prior object-centric manipulation work (Devin et al. 2017, OTTER, DexGraspVLA, GROOT), and the paper's positioning against these closest relatives is thin (OTTER is only discussed qualitatively and not empirically compared).

Headline claims are stronger than the evidence. In the main real-world Franka comparison (Table 2), fine-tuned pi0-FAST (76.56%) clearly outperforms LEGO (66.67%); the abstract's 'outperforming state-of-the-art approaches' claim holds only against zero-shot pi0-FAST and OpenVLA-OFT, and the paper is somewhat evasive about this in the abstract/intro.

Potential unfairness and confounds in baseline comparisons. LEGO relies on privileged task specification at test time (target object bounding box -> SAM 2 -> attention mask, with ground-truth masks in simulation), while VLAs receive only a generic language instruction ('pick the toy'). This is a fundamentally different information regime, and the contribution of DetPool vs. the provided object prior is not disentangled. Different action parameterizations (absolute vs. delta joint control) across baselines further complicate the comparison; Table 16 suggests absolute vs. delta control alone can account for ~20-point gaps.

Evaluation protocol inconsistencies: the success threshold was lowered for OpenVLA-OFT in simulation (0.15 m vs. 0.3 m), indicating the evaluation criteria were adjusted per-method, which raises concerns about protocol uniformity and the reliability of cross-method comparisons.

Statistical rigor is limited: most results lack error bars, seeds, or variance estimates (only Table 6 reports confidence intervals), despite success-rate differences of a few points being interpreted as meaningful (e.g., the 1-4% color-diversity effect in Table 13).

The 'scaling law' claims are based on simulation ablations only, and Figure 4's conclusion that '15 toys is already enough' for robust transfer is surprising and under-supported; the toy-count axis (1/5/15/25/125/250/500/1000) is described but the experimental design for the 500/1000-toy sets is unclear given only 250 toys exist in the main dataset.

DetPool's dependence on SAM 2 plus a separately trained Faster R-CNN detector (trained on manually annotated toy images) is a nontrivial pipeline dependency that may not transfer to the diverse real objects evaluated, and the paper does not analyze detector/mask failure rates on YCB objects at test time.

Generalization claim scope is narrow: only grasping (plus one push-task sim experiment), single-object tabletop scenes, RGB-only, and known limitations (physical properties, single-step tasks) are acknowledged but this limits the significance of 'learning to grasp anything.'

Sim-to-real story is muddled: real data (1,500 Franka demos) is central to the reported real-world results, so the claim of generalization 'from toys' conflates toy training data with substantial in-embodiment real demonstrations.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: whether generalizable grasping can be learned from a small set of randomly composed primitive 'toys', framed convincingly with cognitive science motivation and related work (part-based representations, object-centric learning).
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: simulation (ManiSkill), real Franka on YCB, and a real H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands, covering two different embodiments and gripper/hand types.

Strong ablation suite: pooling alternatives (attention/CLS/mean vs. DetPool), scaling with toy count and demonstrations, model size, primitive types, toy complexity, geometric similarity analysis, and robustness analyses (lighting, clutter, distractors, mask noise) in the appendix.

The central empirical finding—that an object-centric representation induced by masking attention in the ViT drives cross-domain generalization—is well supported: DetPool beats pooling baselines by 22-48% in Table 1, and the scaling trends (demos matter more than toy diversity) are useful findings.

Highly data-efficient (86M params, 1,500 demos) yet competitive with or better than much larger VLA baselines in the zero-shot setting; reproducibility is good (code, checkpoints, dataset, and extensive hardware/training details).
Additional experiments (push-to-target task, comparisons with GROOT/DexGraspVLA/ShapeGrasp) broaden the evidence beyond pure grasping.
weaknesses: Some headline claims are stronger than the evidence: the abstract/conclusion emphasize outperforming state-of-the-art on YCB, but Table 2 shows finetuned π0-FAST (76.56%) clearly beats LEGO (66.67%); LEGO is only second-best on the real Franka benchmark.

DetPool relies on accurate object segmentation masks at inference time (SAM 2 plus a Faster R-CNN trained on only 200 toy images). How this detector reliably segments arbitrary YCB/everyday objects it was not trained on is underexplored, and this pipeline itself may encode much of the generalization; the method's dependence on this detection stack deserves more analysis and a failure analysis.

The technical novelty of DetPool is modest—attention masking + mean pooling over object patches is a simple mechanism—so the contribution rests primarily on the empirical finding and the toy-dataset construction; comparison with the most similar method (OTTER) is only discussed, not empirically compared.

Potential baseline-fairness concerns: baselines appear tuned differently across settings (e.g., π0-FAST uses delta control on H1-2 while LEGO uses absolute control; success threshold lowered for OpenVLA-OFT in simulation), and the non-monotonic degradation of OpenVLA-OFT with more data in Table 1 is unusual and not fully explained.

Real-world evaluation is limited to tabletop single-object grasping with 16 trials/object; variance across objects is not reported for Tables 2-3, and only 5 trials per object for the H1-2 setting limits statistical confidence; known hardware issues with the Inspire hands further constrain the humanoid conclusions.
Generalization scope is narrow: only rigid, single-step grasping; performance on deformable objects, different physical properties, and scenes is acknowledged as unknown but not tested.
